title: Technical debt: deliberate and accidental, prudent and reckless

videos.script: Every engineering team says it has technical debt. Ask which debt, and why it matters, and the answer goes vague. {{title}} The phrase comes from Ward Cunningham, in 1992, and he meant something precise. Shipping code before you fully understand the problem is like taking out a loan. It speeds you up, as long as you pay it back. The danger is the loan nobody repays, because every change to that code pays interest. {{loan}} Martin Fowler later asked two questions about any debt. Was it taken on deliberately, or without noticing? And was it prudent, or reckless? The answers give four kinds of debt. {{quadrant}} Coreto has one of each. The seat-hold locking was a sensible design for small theatres. The flaky test suite was a shortcut the team chose again and again. {{coreto}} By the end of this lesson you can tell real debt from a bug or a matter of taste. You can say which kind it is, and write it in a short register. Lesson five puts a price on it. {{register}}
